extracted.intended_audience: writers of humorous fiction and public speakers; editors and illustrators; general readers interested in Mark Twain's craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples (from Mark Twain's letters and memoir material) about producing humorous prose and public lectures, choosing and overseeing illustrations, editing for tone, and working practices that support sustained creative output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous writer's demeanour: absolute seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The humorous writer pretends to absolute seriousness (when he knows his trade)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present humorous material with a tone of complete seriousness so the reader/audience accepts the frame and the surprise or irony lands. This is presented as a craft rule—affecting how jokes and comic situations should be delivered in prose or speech to preserve their effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration tone: avoid humorous pictures for humorous subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not humorous pictures. No. When they are good (or bad) one's humor gets no chance to play surprises on the reader. A humorous subject illustrated seriously is all right, but a humorous artist is no fit person for such work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a humorous narrative, choose serious or non-comic illustrations so they don't preempt or undercut the writer's controlled surprises. Comic/cartoonish illustrations are an anti-pattern because they reveal the joke and neutralize the prose humor. Example: author requests 'not humorous pictures' for A Horse's Tale and asks for serious photographic-exact reproduction where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author oversight of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Could I be allowed to sit in judgment upon the pictures before they are accepted—at least those in which Cathy may figure?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should request the right to approve illustrations that affect tone or depict key characters, particularly when emotional or personal scenes are involved. Oversight helps ensure illustrations preserve intended tone and do not introduce mismatches or unintended humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture structure: alternate factual 'spoonfuls' with illustrative 'barrels'
rubrics_metrics.description: "first, excite the audience with a spoonful of information about Fulton, then quiet down with a barrel of illustration drawn by memory from my books—and so on and so on... Next, excite the house with another spoonful of Fultonian fact, then tranquilize them again with another barrel of illustration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing a comic lecture, intersperse small, interesting factual morsels with large narrative illustrations or anecdotes. The contrast keeps attention and provides rhythm: brief informational 'spoons' to pique interest, then extended illustrative material to entertain and deepen the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative presentation to persuade audience
rubrics_metrics.description: "And so on and so on, all through the evening; and if you are discreet and don't tell them the illustrations don't illustrate anything, they won't notice it and I will send them home as well-informed about Robert Fulton as I am myself. Don't be afraid; I know all about audiences, they believe everything you say, except when you are telling the truth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an assured, authoritative delivery to make audiences accept claims and enjoy the performance. Twain notes audiences readily believe the speaker; exploit that credulity for comic effect, but be aware the remark about truth is an ironic observation on audience credulity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture timing: adapt length to audience control
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is my custom to keep on talking till I get the audience cowed. Sometimes it takes an hour and fifteen minutes, sometimes I can do it in an hour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rigidly fix talk length; adjust pacing and duration based on how effectively you have engaged or 'cowed' the audience. The performer should read the room and continue while maintaining control and interest—variable durations are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising/Promotion tactic: mark ads 'Private and Confidential'
rubrics_metrics.description: "P.S. Mark all the advertisements 'Private and Confidential,' otherwise the people will not read them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A counterintuitive promotional ploy: label publicity or program notes as 'Private and Confidential' to provoke curiosity and increase readership/attention. Presented as a practical tip for event promotion or printed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive revision to remove degrading or promotional material
rubrics_metrics.description: "I wrote Eve's Diary... I was going to write and ask you to melt the plates and put it out of print. But this morning I examined it without temper, and saw that if I abolished the advertisement it would be literature again. So I have done it. I have struck out 700 words and inserted 5 MS pages of new matter (650 words)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to excise sections (even hundreds of words) that degrade the literary quality (e.g., promotional copy or advertisements embedded in text). Radical cuts and replacement passages can restore a piece's literary integrity; authorial self-editing is emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose style: terse Anglo-Saxon diction for force and compactness
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that Twain's "terse Anglo-Saxon diction" let him put more words on a magazine page and "get more force into what he put on the page."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise Anglo-Saxon-rooted diction (short, strong words) to increase both density (more words per page) and rhetorical force. This stylistic choice is presented as a reason Twain's writing was efficient and powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work environment: prefer views with water and bracing air for productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is my conviction that there should always be some water in a view... The atmosphere of the New Hampshire highlands is exceptionally bracing and stimulating, and a fine aid to hard and continuous work. It is a just claim, I think. I came in May, and wrought 35 successive days without a break."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a workspace with an inspiring view (preferably including water) and a bracing atmosphere to enhance sustained creative productivity. Twain attributes a burst of disciplined writing to the New Hampshire environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match illustration tone to subject seriousness (avoid making tragic subjects comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The remark is funny—because the horse is not aware of it but the fact is not humorous, it is tragic and it is no subject for a humorous picture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to allow illustrations to treat intrinsically tragic or serious elements as comic; doing so can be tonally inappropriate and undermine the work. Tone-matching is crucial: even if a line or remark is funny in context, the underlying fact may be tragic and should be depicted accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing strategy: consider simultaneous magazine rights to broaden reach
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why not sell simultaneous rights, for this once, to the Ladies' Home Journal or Collier's, or both, and recoup yourself?—for I would like to get it to classes that can't afford Harper's."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, sell simultaneous serial rights to multiple periodicals to reach audiences who cannot afford the primary publisher's edition and to increase revenue. Consider accessibility and market reach in publication decisions.
